title: Job loses everything
hook: a good man loses his children, wealth and health (Job 1–2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: eight parts of a path, the Buddha's fourth truth. Your line was one step of eight. Which step did the day hand you? Today the question of suffering moves to another house: the book of Job. Day seven hundred eight.

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." The book opens like a folk tale, plain and quick. And before anything happens to him, it tells us what kind of man he is: "perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." Hold on to that line. The whole book leans on it. The story is about to take everything this man has, and it wants the reader to know, before a single loss, that he did nothing to earn it.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.` → `PERFECT AND UPRIGHT.` → `BEFORE A SINGLE LOSS.`

segments.voice: First, a full house. Job has sons and daughters, flocks and herds, and a large household. His children hold feasts in each other's homes, and afterward Job rises early to make offerings for them, in case one of them sinned in their heart. A careful father, worried for his kids. Second, a scene Job never sees. The story moves to heaven, and a figure the King James calls Satan puts a question to God: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Take away what he has, the figure says, and see what he does. God allows it. Nowhere in the book is Job told about this conversation. Not in chapter one, and not at the end. Third, the messengers. On one day, messengers come running, and each is still speaking when the next arrives. Raiders took the oxen and the donkeys. Fire fell and burned the sheep. Raiders took the camels. And a great wind struck the house where his sons and daughters were eating, and they died. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and says: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Then chapter two takes his body too: sores from the soles of his feet to the top of his head. He sits down among the ashes and scrapes himself with a piece of broken pottery. Fourth, it wasn't deserved. The book tells the reader, and not Job, that none of this is punishment. God himself calls Job his servant, a perfect and an upright man. So whatever explanations arrive in the chapters ahead, the reader has already been told this much. Jews and Christians both read Job as scripture, and they read it in many ways. But the book itself starts here: a good man, and losses he did not earn.
screen: `A FULL HOUSE, A CAREFUL FATHER.` · `A SCENE JOB NEVER SEES.` · `THE MESSENGERS, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `THE READER KNOWS: NOT PUNISHMENT.` · then, large: `IT WASN'T DESERVED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the body be heavy for a moment. Bring to mind someone carrying a pain they didn't earn. An illness, an accident, a loss that came out of nowhere. It might be you. Picture them as the book pictures Job at the end of chapter two: sitting down, in the ashes, with what's left. The reader of Job is told one thing that Job is not. So be that reader for a moment. Over the person you're picturing, say the line inwardly, once, slowly: it wasn't deserved. Then just stay beside them, the way you'd stay beside someone sitting on the ground. The bell holds the time.
Job loses everything: in the opening chapters of Job, a blameless man loses his children, his wealth and his health, and the reader is told it isn't punishment. Today's word.

Your line: it wasn't deserved. Today, if you hear someone blaming themselves for a trouble they didn't cause, or catch yourself doing it, say the line once, aloud or inside: it wasn't deserved. Day seven hundred eight.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians read the book of Job as scripture, and it is often read or studied in times of grief and loss; readers in both traditions interpret its opening in different ways.

original.note: Hebrew: Job, the man from the land of Uz, as his name is written in the Hebrew Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: the book of Job is about a man being punished for something.
what it means: a blameless man loses children, wealth and health, and the book tells the reader first that it wasn't deserved.
what a scholar hears: the book's frame: the reader overhears the heavenly scenes (Job 1:6–12; 2:1–6), and Job never does, so his whole argument happens without them.

notes: Editor: cut the stock line 'here's what the book does that's hard to forget' and the claim that 'every reading' starts from the opening; 'Job is never told' now says 'nowhere in the book is Job told'; 'the reader already knows which one is wrong' softened so day 710's ending isn't pre-echoed.

Job 1:5 paraphrased (offerings for the children 'in case one of them sinned in their heart'); 1:13–19 paraphrased (the messengers and losses); 2:3 and 1:8 paraphrased (God calls Job his servant, perfect and upright); 2:7–8 paraphrased (sores from sole to crown, potsherd, ashes).
The adversary is described as 'a figure the King James calls Satan' to avoid making a claim about the Hebrew term; a Keeper may want a line on how Jewish and Christian readers understand this figure.
Original: אִיּוֹב with pronunciation ee-YOVE; confirm transliteration.
Hook line 'the whole book leans on it' is interpretive.

Audit (2026-10-01): practice and carry rewritten; both had the listener notice the mind hunting for a reason and set it down, which is day 710's practice ('don't explain it') almost word for word. Now the listener stands where the book's reader stands and offers the line 'it wasn't deserved'.
